An app is parts the OS starts and stops, not one main()

AppsThe OS calls your app, step by step
public class MainActivity extends Activity {
void onCreate(Bundle b) { setContentView(...); }
void onStart() { } // visible
void onResume() { } // in front, gets touches
void onPause() { } // leaving the front
void onStop() { } // not visible
void onRestart() { }
void onDestroy() { }
}
The OS drives the app; the app only answers callbacks
Callback order from "The activity lifecycle", Android Developers · class trimmed to its callbacks (each real callback also calls super) · state chain after the lifecycle figure on the same page
AppsThe main thread is one event loop
public static void loop() { // Looper.java
for (;;) {
if (!loopOnce(me, ident, thresholdOverride)) return;
}
}
private static boolean loopOnce(...) {
Message msg = me.mQueue.next(); // might block
if (msg == null) return false;
msg.target.dispatchMessage(msg); // your onClick()
msg.recycleUnchecked();
return true;
}
Never block the main thread: slow work goes to a worker
Looper.java (frameworks/base, AOSP main, Apache 2.0), logging and tracing lines removed · 5-second input timeout: "ANRs", Android Developers · messages in the queue are an example
ProcessesInside Zygote: fork, then specialize
// ZygoteConnection.java: the system asks for one new app
pid = Zygote.forkAndSpecialize(uid, gid, gids, ..., niceName, ...);
if (pid == 0) { // in child
zygoteServer.closeServerSocket();
return handleChildProc(parsedArgs, ...); // -> ActivityThread.main
} else { // in the parent
handleParentProc(pid, serverPipeFd); // send the pid back
}
// com_android_internal_os_Zygote.cpp
pid_t pid = fork(); // in ForkCommon()
if (pid == 0) SpecializeCommon(...); // the child only:
setresgid(gid, gid, gid);
setresuid(uid, uid, uid);
selinux_android_setcontext(uid, ..., se_info, nice_name);
fork gives speed; setuid and SELinux turn the copy into the app
Excerpts of ZygoteConnection.java and com_android_internal_os_Zygote.cpp (frameworks/base, AOSP main, Apache 2.0), argument lists shortened · uid 10123 and the app name are an example
ProcessesLow on memory? Kill, don't swap
Android frees memory by killing the least important app first
Scores: constants in ProcessList.java (frameworks/base, AOSP main, Apache 2.0): SYSTEM_ADJ -900, FOREGROUND 0, PERCEPTIBLE 200, SERVICE 500, HOME 600, PREVIOUS 700, CACHED 900-999 · memory levels and apps are an example
ProcessesKilling an app takes up to 40 tries
int killProcessGroup(uid_t uid, int initialPid, int signal, int* max_processes) {
return KillProcessGroup(uid, initialPid, signal, 40 /*retries*/, max_processes);
}
static int KillProcessGroup(uid_t uid, int initialPid, int signal, int retries,
int* max_processes) {
int retry = retries;
int processes;
while ((processes = DoKillProcessGroupOnce(cgroup, uid, initialPid, signal)) > 0) {
if (retry > 0) {
std::this_thread::sleep_for(5ms);
--retry;
} else {
break;
}
}
if (processes == 0) { ... RemoveProcessGroup(cgroup, uid, initialPid, retries); }
A process can fork while it is being killed, so the killer loops
processgroup.cpp, libprocessgroup, tag android-12.0.0_r3 (Apache 2.0), logging lines removed; newer releases wait on the cgroup instead of fixed 5 ms sleeps · pids are an example · keeping apps alive through such races: EuroSys 2019 (doi 10.1145/3302424.3303956)
SandboxOne Linux user per app
// android_filesystem_config.h
#define AID_APP_START 10000 /* first app user */
#define AID_APP_END 19999 /* last app user */
// in the Chat app, uid 10102:
int fd = open("/data/data/com.bank/files/token", O_RDONLY);
// fd == -1, errno == EACCES: Permission denied
A user ID per app turns old UNIX file permissions into a sandbox
AID_APP_START and AID_APP_END from android_filesystem_config.h (system/core, AOSP main, Apache 2.0) · "Application sandbox", source.android.com · apps, uids and the file are an example

BinderApps ask system services for everything
Like a microkernel: services in user space, talking by messages
After "Platform architecture" and "Binder IPC", Android Developers and source.android.com · Binder as a "microkernel" style API: the earlier Lecture 25 slides · monolithic vs microkernel: Lecture 3
BinderOne Binder call, hop by hop
// app: proxy code generated from the AIDL interface
_data.writeInterfaceToken(DESCRIPTOR);
mRemote.transact(Stub.TRANSACTION_getLocation, _data, _reply, 0);
// libbinder: IPCThreadState.cpp
err = writeTransactionData(BC_TRANSACTION, flags, handle, code, data, nullptr);
err = waitForResponse(reply); // -> talkWithDriver()
ioctl(mProcess->mDriverFD, BINDER_WRITE_READ, &bwr)
// kernel: the binder driver
// copy the data once, into the service's mapped buffer; wake a thread
// service: a binder thread from its pool
onTransact(code, data, reply, flags); // run the method, write the reply
A Binder call is an ioctl on /dev/binder: one copy, one waiting thread
IPCThreadState.cpp (frameworks/native, AOSP main, Apache 2.0) · proxy lines in the form AIDL generates; getLocation is an example method · one-copy design: "Binder IPC", source.android.com
